public evening on permissioning, shared space, and what it takes to keep civic technology alive once the first funding ends.","type":"text"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Cities build civic technology that works. Systems that book spaces, route permits, and coordinate community use of shared infrastructure. Many of them stop working. Not because the technology failed. Because nobody built the structure to keep them alive once the initial funding ended. That is not a Korean problem, or a London problem, or a Berlin problem. It is a structural one.","type":"text"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"There is a nightclub in Berlin that is world-famous from Friday night to Monday morning. Berlin clubs open at midnight and run until morning; the floor is empty every weekday from dawn until the doors open again. That is roughly 60 hours a week of a large, warm space with a sound system, open floor, and chairs sitting unused. A language exchange group needs somewhere on Tuesday mornings. A youth theatre wants a rehearsal room on Wednesday afternoons. A repair café, a dance course, a community kitchen: the uses are not hard to imagine. The venue owner is open to it. The problem is not goodwill. It is that no system exists to generate a conditional agreement across different use types, risk profiles, and insurance requirements at any useful speed. So the space stays empty.","type":"text"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Civic Ledger is one attempt to close that gap. Built with Dark Matter Labs across South Korea, London, and Melbourne, it converts plain-language civic requests into structured, conditional agreements that cities and communities operate together. It has been tested across more than 40 spaces in Incheon, Yongin, and Jeollanam-do. In December 2026, its R&D funding ends. What comes next is not a technology question. It is a governance, licensing, and sustainability question that every city running public-interest digital infrastructure will eventually face.","type":"text"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Berlin is not the destination for those questions. It is a co-contributor. Berlin's new climate adaptation law is live, contested, and in need of coordination infrastructure. Its district-level data governance work is active. Its civic-tech ecosystem has its own hard experience of what happens when civic agreements break under political pressure. The problems Civic Ledger surfaces in South Korea, including who governs civic data, what legal form can hold public-interest infrastructure, and how open licensing protects without blocking reuse, are problems Berlin is already working on from its own direction.","type":"text"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"This evening is the first public moment of that exchange. It is a working conversation, not a product launch. We are looking for people who can contribute to both sides: funders and investors who want to understand civic infrastructure as an asset class, city actors and commissioners who manage shared space, and practitioners working at the edges of governance, legal design, and public-interest technology.","type":"text"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"What to expect","type":"text","marks":[{"type":"bold"}]}]},{"type":"bullet_list","content":[{"type":"list_item","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Opening framing: why civic infrastructure fails after first funding and what a shared alternative looks like","type":"text"}]}]},{"type":"list_item","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Live platform demonstration using the Berlin nightclub case","type":"text"}]}]},{"type":"list_item","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Discussion of the governance, licensing, and sustainability challenge","type":"text"}]}]},{"type":"list_item","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Facilitated conversations","type":"text"}]}]},{"type":"list_item","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Drinks and informal exchange","type":"text"}]}]}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"text":"Hosted by Dark Matter Labs and Politics for Tomorrow/nextLearning.
